propositions.text: Ensuring payment and liquidity for contractors and subcontractors is a significant concern in construction.
propositions.quote: Ensuring payment of contractors and subcontractors and encouraging liquidity in the flow of funds to them are both significant preoccupations in the construction industry.

propositions.text: Two statutory remedies protect those providing services or materials: construction liens and statutory trusts.
propositions.quote: two statutory remedies have been developed in provincial legislation to protect those who provide services or materials to a project: construction liens (also known as mechanic’s or builder’s liens) and statutory trusts.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that payment and liquidity for contractors are important, and two statutory remedies exist: liens and trusts.

propositions.text: The Court must consider the interaction between lien bonds and trust obligations under Manitoba's Builders’ Liens Act.
propositions.quote: This case requires the Court to consider the interaction between these two statutory remedies in the Manitoba Builders’ Liens Act, C.C.S.M., c. B91 (“BLA” or “Act”). Specifically, by filing a lien bond in court in order to vacate a builder’s lien, has a contractor satisfied its trust obligations with respect to the subcontractors who have registered liens against the land upon which the construction work was being done?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue: whether filing a lien bond satisfies trust obligations under the BLA.

propositions.text: The BLA is silent on the interaction of lien bonds and trust obligations, but they are separate remedies.
propositions.quote: The BLA is silent as to how these provisions interact. However, the text and context of the provisions, as well as the history of the Act, reveal that these are two separate remedies for unpaid persons who have done work, provided services, or supplied materials for a construction project.

propositions.text: Registering a lien bond does not relieve a contractor of trust obligations under the BLA; appeal should be dismissed.
propositions.quote: Registering a lien bond does not relieve a contractor of its trust obligations under the BLA. This appeal should be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds lien bonds and trust obligations are separate; registering a lien bond does not relieve trust obligations; appeal dismissed.

propositions.text: Dominion was hired as general contractor to build Investors Group Field stadium in December 2010.
propositions.quote: In December 2010, Dominion Construction Company Inc. (“Dominion”, now known as Stuart Olson Dominion Construction Ltd.) was hired by BBB Stadium Inc. (“Owner”) as general contractor to construct Investors Group Field, a new football stadium at the University of Manitoba.

propositions.text: In April 2011, Dominion subcontracted Structal to supply and install steel for $44,435,383.
propositions.quote: In April 2011, Dominion entered into a subcontract with Structal Heavy Steel (“Structal”) under which Structal would supply and install steel for the structure, roof, bleachers, and wall of the stadium for $44,435,383.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Dominion was hired as general contractor and subcontracted Structal for steel work for $44 million.

propositions.text: Dominion withheld payment from Structal starting April 2012, initially blaming Owner's delay.
propositions.quote: Beginning with the April 2012 billing, Dominion withheld payment from Structal, originally citing the Owner’s delay in paying Dominion.

propositions.text: In August, Dominion said unpaid amounts were used for back charges due to Structal's delays.
propositions.quote: However, in August, Dominion advised that it was using the unpaid amounts for back charges it claimed resulted from delays attributable to Structal.

paragraphs.summary: Dominion withheld payments from Structal starting April 2012, first blaming Owner, then citing back charges for delays.

propositions.text: Structal registered a builder’s lien for $15,570,974.53 on Sept 7, 2012, covering invoices, holdback, and delay claim.
propositions.quote: On September 7, 2012, Structal registered a builder’s lien against the property totalling $15,570,974.53 — $3,538,029.97 for past-due invoices; $633,885.28 for invoices falling due on October 1, 2012; $3,331,500.69 for statutory holdback, and an $8,067,558.59 delay claim.

propositions.text: Dominion filed a lien bond in court on Oct 22, 2012, covering the full lien amount, securing payment if judgment not satisfied.
propositions.quote: On October 22, 2012, Dominion filed a lien bond in the full amount of the builder’s lien in the Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench. This bond provided that if Dominion did not satisfy any lien judgment against it, the surety of the bond would pay, up to a maximum, the amount of the judgment.

paragraphs.summary: Structal registered a lien for over $15 million; Dominion filed a lien bond covering full amount to vacate lien.

propositions.text: Structal approved the bond and vacated its lien; Dominion continued receiving progress payments.
propositions.quote: Structal approved the bond and vacated its lien. Dominion continued to receive progress payments from the Owner.

propositions.text: Structal asserted Dominion must comply with the trust provisions of the Act.
propositions.quote: Structal asserted that Dominion was required to comply with the trust provisions of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Structal approved the bond and vacated lien but asserted Dominion must comply with trust provisions.

propositions.text: Dominion refused further payments to Structal, claiming set-off, no breach of trust, and lien bond security.
propositions.quote: Nonetheless, Dominion refused to make further payments to Structal, maintaining that it had a set-off against the monies claimed by Structal, that there was no breach of trust, and that Structal was fully secured by the lien bond.

paragraphs.summary: Dominion refused further payments, claiming set-off, no trust breach, and lien bond security.

propositions.text: Structal requested Owner withhold $3,538,029.97 from Dominion or face trust violation action; Owner complied.
propositions.quote: Structal responded by requesting that the Owner withhold a $3,538,029.97 payment from Dominion or face an action for violating the trust provisions of the BLA. The Owner obliged

propositions.text: Dominion applied to Court for declaration it satisfied BLA trust obligations to Structal to pay withheld amount elsewhere.
propositions.quote: Dominion brought an application in the Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench seeking a declaration that it had satisfied its BLA trust obligations to Structal. If granted, it could pay the amount the Owner was withholding to other trust claimants and, once satisfied, to other creditors.

propositions.text: Structal filed motion requiring full payment of past-due invoices without set-off upon Dominion receiving funds.
propositions.quote: Structal then filed its own motion requiring full payment of its past-due invoices, without deduction or set-off, upon Dominion receiving the funds from the Owner.

paragraphs.summary: Structal requested Owner withhold payment; Dominion sought declaration it satisfied trust obligations; Structal demanded full payment without set-off.

propositions.text: Court of Queen’s Bench ruled lien bond secured Structal’s trust claim; Owner paid $4,171,915.25 to Dominion.
propositions.quote: Schulman J. of the Court of Queen’s Bench ruled that the lien bond secured Structal’s trust claim, whereupon the sum of $4,171,915.25 was paid by the Owner to Dominion on account of Structal’s completed and certified work (R.F., at para. 19).

propositions.text: Dominion used funds to pay other contractors and itself; Structal paid all subcontractors from own resources.
propositions.quote: Dominion used these funds to pay other contractors and itself. Structal has paid all its subcontractors in full from its own resources ($3,950,849.26 in payments) and its subcontract has been certified for payment.

paragraphs.summary: Court ruled lien bond secured trust claim; Owner paid Dominion; Dominion paid others; Structal paid subcontractors itself.

propositions.text: Filing lien bond extinguished Dominion’s trust obligations to Structal under BLA.
propositions.quote: In the Court of Queen’s Bench, Schulman J. ruled that Dominion’s filing of the lien bond extinguished its trust obligations to Structal under the BLA.

propositions.text: No indication in BLA that contractor must pay twice: once to vacate lien and again for trust.
propositions.quote: He wrote that there is no indication in the BLA “that a general contractor in the position of [Dominion] should pay the amount in issue twice, once in vacating the lien and another time in securing the trust” (para. 18).

propositions.text: Requiring payment twice would be commercially unreasonable and contrary to legislation intent.
propositions.quote: It would be “commercially unreasonable and contrary to the intention of the legislation to require [Dominion] in effect to pay $8,000,000 to secure payment of Structal’s claim for $4,000,000” (para. 18).

paragraphs.summary: Court of Queen’s Bench found lien bond extinguished trust obligations; paying twice would be unreasonable and contrary to intent.

propositions.text: Lien bond stands in place of lien, securing amount claimed by Structal.
propositions.quote: Schulman J. maintained that the lien bond filed by Dominion “stands in place of the lien, securing the sum of money claimed by Structal” (para. 17).

propositions.text: Lien bond extinguished statutory trust obligations; Dominion may disburse progress payments without breach.
propositions.quote: As such, the lien bond filed by Dominion had extinguished its statutory trust obligations to Structal, and “upon receipt of the progress payment in question in this case [Dominion] may disburse the funds without being in breach of the trust provisions of the [BLA]” (para. 24).

paragraphs.summary: Court of Queen’s Bench found lien bond extinguished trust obligations; Dominion may disburse payments without breach.

propositions.text: Manitoba Court of Appeal overturned Court of Queen’s Bench on lien bond extinguishing trust obligations.
propositions.quote: Writing for a unanimous Court of Appeal panel, MacInnes J.A. overturned Schulman J.’s holding with respect to the lien bond extinguishing Dominion’s trust obligations to Structal.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal overturned lower court's finding that lien bond extinguished trust obligations.

propositions.text: Under BLA, subcontractors have two distinct rights: statutory trust and lien claim against property.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal concluded that under the BLA, subcontractors have two separate and distinct rights beyond the common law right to sue for breach of contract: the right to the statutory trust and the right to file a lien claim against the property (ss. 4 to 9).

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal found subcontractors have two distinct rights: statutory trust and lien claim.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal allowed Structal’s appeal and set aside motion judge’s order.
propositions.quote: MacInnes J.A. allowed Structal’s appeal and set aside the order of the motion judge.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal allowed Structal’s appeal and set aside lower court order.

propositions.text: Dominion claims trust provisions apply only to subcontractors whose claims might not be protected by lien.
propositions.quote: Dominion claims that the trust provisions apply only for “sub-contractors whose claims might not be protected by lien” (A.F., at para. 40).

propositions.text: Whether trust provisions apply to subcontractors whose claims are protected by lien is a statutory interpretation question.
propositions.quote: Evaluation of this assertion involves consideration of the relationship between the lien and trust provisions of the BLA. The application of the trust provisions to those contractors or subcontractors whose claims are protected by a lien is a question of statutory interpretation which can be answered with regard to the legislative evolution, text, and context of the provisions.

paragraphs.summary: Dominion argues trust provisions apply only to subcontractors without lien protection; court frames this as statutory interpretation issue.

propositions.text: It is necessary to outline each provision in its own right first.
propositions.quote: It is first necessary to outline each of the provisions in their own right.

paragraphs.summary: Court states it will first outline each provision separately.

propositions.text: Section 13 BLA grants lien rights to persons who do work, provide services, or supply materials under contract.
propositions.quote: The right of lien against the interest of the owner of the land or structure is set out in s. 13 of the BLA. This remedy is available to persons who do any work, provide any services, or supply materials in performance of a contract or sub-contract for any owner, contractor or sub-contractor has, by virtue thereof, a lien for the value of the work, services or materials which, subject to section 16, attaches upon the estate or interest of the owner in the land or structure upon or in respect of which the work was done or the services were provided or the materials were supplied, and the land occupied thereby or enjoyed therewith.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains s.13 BLA grants lien rights to those performing work or supplying materials under contract.

propositions.text: Lien creates charge against land for contractors, suppliers, and workers who prove claims.
propositions.quote: As the Manitoba Court of Appeal explained in Provincial Drywall Supply Ltd. v. Gateway Construction Co. (1993), 85 Man. R. (2d) 116, the purpose of the lien is to “creat[e] charges against the land in favour of those contractors, suppliers and workers who can prove their claims” (para. 47).

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Manitoba Court of Appeal that lien creates charge against land for claimants who prove claims.

propositions.text: Lien encumbers land; mortgage advances after lien registration are stalled.
propositions.quote: When a lien is registered, it encumbers the land on which the work was done or the structure with respect to which the work was done (BLA, s. 13). Because a lien creates an encumbrance on the land, mortgage advances subsequent to registration of a lien are typically stalled when liens are filed.

propositions.text: Act allows vacating liens by posting security or payment into court, typically a lien bond.
propositions.quote: Recognizing this impediment to liquidity, the Act provides for vacating the liens, pending resolution of the validity of the lien claims, if alternative security is posted. Section 55(2) provides that a lien may be vacated upon payment into or the filing of security (typically a lien bond) with the court

paragraphs.summary: Court explains lien encumbers land and can be vacated by posting security or payment into court.

propositions.text: Section 56(1) provides money or security paid into court stands in place of the land against which the lien was registered.
propositions.quote: Section 56(1) then provides that any money or security paid into court stands in place of the land: 56(1) Any money paid into court or any security given under subsection 55(2) stands in place of the land against which the lien was registered

propositions.text: Money or security paid into court is subject to claims of persons whose liens have been vacated and those with subsisting claims who registered prior to payment out application.
propositions.quote: and is subject to the claims of (a) the persons whose liens have been vacated; and (b) every person who (i) both at the time of filing the application under subsection 55(2) and at the time of filing application for payment out under subsection (3), has a subsisting claim for lien, and (ii) has registered a claim for lien prior to the time of filing the application for payment out under subsection (3)

propositions.text: Persons whose liens have been vacated have a first charge on the money or security to the extent of amounts found owing by the judge.
propositions.quote: but the persons whose liens have been ordered vacated have a first charge on the money or security to the extent of any amount, including costs, found by the judge to be owing to them.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 56(1) that money or security paid into court replaces the land and is subject to lien claims, with vacated lien holders having first charge.

propositions.text: Payment of money or security into court secures interests of lien registrants by standing in place of the land.
propositions.quote: The function of the payment of money or security into the court is to take the place of the land in securing the interests of the contractor or subcontractor who registered the lien.

propositions.text: The motion judge stated security paid into court stands 'in place of the lien'.
propositions.quote: The motion judge stated that security paid into court would stand “in place of the lien” (para. 17 (emphasis added)).

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal found s. 56(1) unambiguously states security stands in place of the land, not the lien.
propositions.quote: However, as the Court of Appeal found, the text of s. 56(1) is unambiguous that the security paid into court stands in place of the land against which the lien was registered.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains payment into court replaces the land, not the lien, correcting the motion judge's statement per the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: When a lien is registered and security paid into court, the lien registration may be vacated, freeing the land from encumbrance.
propositions.quote: When a lien is registered against the land and security is paid into court, the registration of the lien may be ordered vacated.

propositions.text: Vacating the lien frees the land so mortgage funds can flow for further development.
propositions.quote: The result is that the land is freed from the lien encumbrance and funds, typically mortgage funds, can flow for further development on the land.

propositions.text: The underlying lien claim remains; security paid into court replaces the land as available funds for lien judgment.
propositions.quote: The underlying lien claim, however, remains. The only effect is that the security paid into court, rather than the land, is available in the event of a lien judgment in favour of the contractor or subcontractor.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains vacating a lien frees land but underlying lien claim remains, with security in court replacing land for lien judgment.

propositions.text: The Manitoba Law Reform Commission in 1979 expressed concern to expedite disposition of lien claims once liens are vacated.
propositions.quote: The Manitoba Law Reform Commission in its 1979 Report on Mechanics’ Liens Legislation in Manitoba (“Commission Report”) had expressed concern that there is “a pressing need to expedite the disposition of claims of lienholders once their liens are vacated from the title” (p. 113).

propositions.text: It is costly to pay lien bond premiums or have money tied up in court; BLA signals lien actions should proceed promptly.
propositions.quote: It is a commercial reality in the construction industry that it can prove costly to pay lien bond premiums or to have money tied up in court. The BLA signals that lien actions should proceed promptly.

propositions.text: Once lien is vacated, claimant's charge against money or security ceases if no action commenced within 30 days of notice.
propositions.quote: Once the lien has been vacated, the claimant’s charge against the money paid into court or against the security given ceases to exist if no action is commenced within 30 days of the lien claimants being given notice to commence their action (ss. 49 to 51).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the 1979 Commission's concern to expedite lien claims, costs of bonds, and BLA's 30-day action requirement after lien vacating.

propositions.text: BLA requires a statutory holdback of 7.5% of contract price or work value, retained for at least 40 days after performance milestones.
propositions.quote: Whoever is primarily liable for payment under a contract ... must deduct and retain 7.5 percent of the contract price ... These funds must be retained for at least 40 days after a certificate of substantial performance is given, the work under the contract has been completed, or the work under the contract has been abandoned, whichever occurs first (s. 24(1)).

propositions.text: The holdback fund satisfies lien claims up to its amount and allows subcontractors to be paid directly from the owner despite no privity of contract.
propositions.quote: The holdback is the fund from which lien claims can be satisfied, up to the amount of the holdback. It allows subcontractors to be paid directly from the owner, despite the lack of privity of contract

propositions.text: Bristow et al. explain holdback purpose and operation in construction lien law.
propositions.quote: (D. I. Bristow et al., Construction, Builders’ and Mechanics’ Liens in Canada (7th ed. (loose-leaf)), vol. 1, at pp. 4-3 and 4-4).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains BLA's 7.5% holdback retained for 40 days to satisfy lien claims and allow direct subcontractor payment.

propositions.text: BLA trust provisions in ss. 4 to 9 require subcontractors, workers, and others be paid before owner or contractor can appropriate trust funds.
propositions.quote: The trust provisions of the BLA are found in ss. 4 to 9. They provide that subcontractors, any workers employed by the contractor, and other beneficiaries are to be paid before an owner or contractor can appropriate trust funds for his or her own use.

paragraphs.summary: The court states BLA trust provisions require payment to subcontractors and workers before owner or contractor can use trust funds.

propositions.text: Under s. 4(1), funds received by contractor on contract price are trust funds for subcontractors, Workers’ Compensation Board, workers, and owner for set-offs.
propositions.quote: Under s. 4(1), funds received by a contractor on account of a contract price constitute a trust fund for the benefit of (a) sub-contractors ... (b) the Workers’ Compensation Board; (c) workers ...; and (d) the owner for any set-off or counterclaim relating to the performance of the contract.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 4(1) makes contractor's contract funds trust funds benefiting subcontractors, workers, Workers’ Compensation Board, and owner for set-offs.

propositions.text: Under s. 4(2), funds received by subcontractor on subcontract price are trust funds for subcontractors, Workers’ Compensation Board, workers, and contractor or subcontractor for set-offs.
propositions.quote: Similarly, under s. 4(2), funds received by a subcontractor on account of a contract price in the subcontract constitute a trust fund for the benefit of (a) sub-contractors ... (b) the Workers’ Compensation Board; (c) workers ...; and (d) the contractor or any sub-contractor for any set-off or counterclaim relating to the performance of the sub-contract.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 4(2) makes subcontractor's subcontract funds trust funds benefiting subcontractors, workers, Workers’ Compensation Board, and contractor for set-offs.

propositions.text: Under s. 4(3), contractor cannot appropriate trust funds until all subcontractors, Workers’ Compensation Board, workers, and other beneficiaries are paid or provided for.
propositions.quote: Under s. 4(3), a contractor in possession of trust funds under s. 4(1) cannot appropriate or convert those funds ... until (a) all sub-contractors ... have been paid ...; (b) the Workers’ Compensation Board has been paid ...; (c) all workers ... have been paid ...; and (d) provision has been made for the payment of other affected beneficiaries ...

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 4(3) prohibits contractor from using trust funds until all subcontractors, workers, Workers’ Compensation Board, and beneficiaries are paid or provided for.

propositions.text: Under s. 5(1), funds payable by owner to contractor on payment certifier's certificate are trust funds for contractor, subcontractors, Workers’ Compensation Board, and workers.
propositions.quote: Where, under a contract, sums become payable to the contractor by the owner on the basis of a certificate of a payment certifier, any amount ... constitutes ... a trust fund for the benefit of (a) the contractor and all sub-contractors ...; (b) The Workers’ Compensation Board; and (c) workers ...

propositions.text: Under s. 5(2), all sums received by owner for financing a structure or land improvement, including purchase price and payments for discharge of prior encumbrances, are trust funds for those beneficiaries.
propositions.quote: All sums received by an owner that are to be used in the financing of a structure or improving land, including the purchase price of the land and payment for the discharge or withdrawal of prior encumbrances against the land, constitute ... a trust fund for the benefit of the persons mentioned in subsection (1).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains ss. 5(1) and (2) make owner funds payable to contractor and for financing a structure trust funds for contractor, subcontractors, workers, and Workers’ Compensation Board.

propositions.text: Under s. 5(3), owner may not appropriate trust funds until contractor is paid all sums owed and provision made for other beneficiaries.
propositions.quote: Like a contractor, the owner may not appropriate or convert trust funds or use them for any purpose not authorized by the trust until 5(3) . . . (a) the contractor has been paid all sums justly owed to him ...; and (b) provision for the payment of other affected beneficiaries of the trust has been made.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 5(3) prohibits owner from using trust funds until contractor and other beneficiaries are paid or provided for.

propositions.text: Trust and lien provisions are separate remedies; trust remedy is more wide-reaching and includes more beneficiaries.
propositions.quote: The trust and lien provisions of the BLA are two separate remedies, with the trust remedy being more wide-reaching.

propositions.text: Trust funds cannot be appropriated until all subcontractors and suppliers are paid; lien provisions do not impose such obligations.
propositions.quote: Trust funds, on the other hand, cannot be appropriated for other purposes until all subcontractors and all persons who have supplied materials or services have been paid (s. 4(3)(a)).

propositions.text: No lien can encumber Crown interests, but trust provisions have no such exclusion.
propositions.quote: Moreover, pursuant to s. 16 no lien can encumber the interest of the Crown, a Crown agency, or a municipality. There is no similar exclusion with respect to the trust provisions of the Act (see s. 3(1)).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains trust and lien provisions are separate, trust is broader, and lien excludes Crown interests unlike trust provisions.

propositions.text: Trust provisions were formerly in Builders and Workers Act; lien provisions in Mechanics’ Liens Act; both repealed and incorporated into BLA in 1981.
propositions.quote: The trust provisions were formerly provided for in The Builders and Workers Act ... while the lien provisions were provided for in The Mechanics’ Liens Act ... These two acts were repealed and essentially incorporated into the BLA ... in 1981 as a result of the 1979 Commission Report (Provincial Drywall, at para. 22).

propositions.text: Legislature did not expressly delineate how lien and trust provisions interact when both remedies are pursued concurrently.
propositions.quote: However, in consolidating these two acts, the legislature did not expressly delineate how the lien and trust provisions were to interact in situations such as this case, where both remedies are pursued at the same time by a contractor or subcontractor.

paragraphs.summary: The court states trust and lien provisions were consolidated into BLA in 1981 without expressly delineating their interaction when pursued concurrently.

propositions.text: Dominion asserts trust provisions have narrow purpose to provide security to subcontractors whose claims might not be protected by lien.
propositions.quote: Dominion asserts that the trust provisions of the BLA have a narrow purpose: “. . . to provide security to sub-contractors whose claims might not be protected by lien” (A.F., at para. 40).

paragraphs.summary: Dominion argues trust provisions narrowly secure subcontractors whose claims might not be protected by lien.

propositions.text: Neither BLA text nor Commission Report supports Dominion's narrow purpose assertion; trust remedy originated without lien mechanism and remains independent.
propositions.quote: Neither the text of the BLA nor the Commission Report supports Dominion’s assertion (see A.F., at para. 40). The trust remedy originated in a statute that did not provide a lien mechanism and it was not altered to limit its applicability when both were incorporated into the BLA. Rather, both remedies exist independently.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects Dominion's narrow purpose claim, finding trust remedy independent and not limited by lien provisions.

propositions.text: Canadian Bank of Commerce v. T. McAvity & Sons held lien exemption for public streets applies only to lien, not trust provisions.
propositions.quote: This Court has recognized the distinct operation of lien and trust provisions. In Canadian Bank of Commerce v. T. McAvity & Sons, Ltd., ... held that ... a provision exempting public streets ... applied only to the lien provisions, not the trust provisions.

propositions.text: Preventing lien on public highway avoids private debt sale; denying trust would leave workers without security.
propositions.quote: Preventing a lien from attaching to a public highway served an important purpose: “. . . the sale of a highway to realize a private debt is not to be seriously contemplated” ... denying the statutory trust ... “would defeat [the] fundamental object of the statute ... and leave them without any security whatever”

propositions.text: The two securities, land and money, are completely independent.
propositions.quote: He found that “[t]he two securities, that is, the land and the money, are completely independent of one another”

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Canadian Bank of Commerce v. T. McAvity & Sons to show lien and trust provisions operate distinctly and independently.

propositions.text: BLA s. 66 contemplates concurrent pursuit of lien and trust claims; trust claims not limited to those without lien claims.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the BLA itself contemplates that the lien and trust remedies may be pursued concurrently. Section 66 provides that “a claim related to a trust fund ... may be brought or joined with an action to realize a lien”.

propositions.text: If trust only protected those without lien claims, concurrent claims and s. 66 would have no application; legislature does not enact meaningless provisions.
propositions.quote: If the trust provisions only protected those without a lien claim, there would never be concurrent claims and s. 66 would have no application. The legislature cannot be presumed to enact superfluous or meaningless provisions

paragraphs.summary: The court explains BLA s. 66 allows concurrent lien and trust claims, rejecting any notion trust only protects those without lien claims.

propositions.text: Lien and trust provisions remain separate remedies; claimant may have both claims and access to both remedies.
propositions.quote: Nothing in the BLA suggests that the lien and trust provisions do not remain as two separate remedies. ... the claimant has access to both of these remedies.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes lien and trust provisions are separate remedies and claimants may pursue both concurrently.

propositions.text: Dominion argues filing a lien bond should stand as security for any potential claim, affecting trust remedy.
propositions.quote: Dominion argues that where a lien bond has been filed with the court, the bond should stand as security for any potential claim.

propositions.text: Filing a lien bond has no effect on existence or application of trust remedy under BLA.
propositions.quote: However, a reading of both the lien and trust provisions of the BLA reveals that the filing of a lien bond has no effect on the existence and application of the trust remedy.

paragraphs.summary: Dominion argues lien bond filing should secure claims; the court finds it does not affect trust remedy existence or application.

propositions.text: Manitoba Court of Appeal in Provincial Drywall stated trust provisions ensure money flows according to contractual rights and is not diverted.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the statutory trust was articulated by the Manitoba Court of Appeal in Provincial Drywall: “The trust provisions are designed to help assure that money payable by owners, contractors and subcontractors flows in a manner which is in accord with the contractual rights of those engaged in a building project and it is not diverted out of the proper pipeline” (para. 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Provincial Drywall that trust provisions ensure money flows per contractual rights and is not diverted improperly.

propositions.text: A trust claim is not extinguished by filing a lien bond because the lien bond only secures the lien claim, not the trust claim.
propositions.quote: A lien bond provides no more security than the lien which it displaced: the lien claimant must be successful in the lien action in order to collect the amount secured by the lien bond.

propositions.text: If a lien is invalidated, the lien bond liability is extinguished but the trust claim remains independent and unsecured by the bond.
propositions.quote: If a judgment were to issue invalidating the lien because the lien failed to comply with the requirements in ss. 37 to 45 of the BLA, liability under the lien bond would be extinguished.

propositions.text: If filing a lien bond extinguished trust obligations, claimants would lose both lien and trust claims if the lien failed, disrupting fund flow in construction.
propositions.quote: If Dominion were correct that the mere filing of the lien bond extinguished a contractor’s or owner’s trust obligations... the claimant would be left with no lien claim and no trust monies if the lien claim failed.

propositions.text: The trust provisions were designed to prevent interruption of fund flow down the construction pyramid from owner to subcontractors and suppliers.
propositions.quote: Such interruption of the flow of funds down the so-called construction pyramid... is the very problem that the trust provisions were designed to address.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that filing a lien bond does not extinguish trust claims, which remain independent and protect fund flow in construction.

propositions.text: Dominion posted security in court under s. 55(2) of the BLA, which addresses only the lien claim and does not eliminate the trust.
propositions.quote: Dominion posted security in the court under s. 55(2) of the BLA. The text of this subsection speaks only to the lien claim; nothing in this provision eliminates the trust.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Dominion posted security under s. 55(2) BLA, which pertains only to the lien claim and does not eliminate the trust.

propositions.text: Filing a lien does not affect the statutory trust, consistent with s. 4(3) of the Act barring diversion of trust funds until subcontractors are paid.
propositions.quote: That the filing of the lien has no effect on the subsistence of the statutory trust is consistent with s. 4(3) of the Act...

propositions.text: A subcontractor is not paid by filing a lien or posting security to vacate the lien; a lien bond secures but does not satisfy the lien claim.
propositions.quote: A subcontractor has not been paid simply by the filing of a lien or by funds or security being posted with the court for the purpose of vacating the lien.

propositions.text: A lien bond does not extinguish owner or contractor obligations under the statutory trust.
propositions.quote: It does not extinguish the owner’s or contractor’s obligations under the statutory trust.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds filing a lien or posting security does not satisfy payment or extinguish statutory trust obligations under s. 4(3).

propositions.text: Dominion argues paying funds into court to vacate a lien does not satisfy trust provisions, risking double payment for same work.
propositions.quote: Dominion submits that unless paying funds into court to vacate the lien does not at the same time satisfy the trust provisions... a contractor or owner could be required to pay the funds twice.

propositions.text: Dominion cites L. W. Bennett Co. v. University of Western Ontario to argue law forbids paying money twice under court sanction.
propositions.quote: Dominion argues... the law will never compel a person to pay a sum of money a second time which he has paid once under the sanction of the court.

paragraphs.summary: Dominion argues paying funds into court to vacate a lien risks double payment, citing precedent forbidding paying money twice under court sanction.

propositions.text: Dominion's argument confuses payment with security; funds posted to vacate liens do not constitute payment to lien claimants.
propositions.quote: Dominion’s argument blurs the distinction between payment and security. Should an owner or contractor pay funds into or post security with the court... such funds or security do not constitute payment to the lien claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Dominion confuses payment with security; posting funds to vacate liens is not payment to claimants.

propositions.text: Contractors may maintain double security by posting a lien bond while holding trust funds, but can avoid this by paying cash into court under s. 55(2).
propositions.quote: There may be circumstances where a contractor will choose to maintain double security... However, a contractor can avoid double security by paying cash into court pursuant to s. 55(2) instead of depositing a lien bond.

propositions.text: The BLA prohibits appropriation or conversion of trust funds until certain steps occur (ss. 4(3), 4(4), 5(3)).
propositions.quote: The BLA provides that any owner, contractor, or subcontractor with trust obligations “shall not appropriate or convert any part of the trust fund... until one of the listed steps has occurred (ss. 4(3), 4(4) and 5(3)).

propositions.text: Paying trust funds into court to vacate a lien does not appropriate or convert trust funds; funds remain impressed with the trust.
propositions.quote: Payment of the trust funds into court to vacate a lien... does not constitute an appropriation or conversion of the trust funds.

propositions.text: If the lien claim fails, trust funds paid into court remain trust funds when returned to owner, contractor, or subcontractor.
propositions.quote: Should the lien claim fail while the trust claim is outstanding, the cash would continue to be trust funds when returned to the owner, contractor, or subcontractor.

propositions.text: Trust funds deposited with the court remain secure and the trust is not breached.
propositions.quote: So long as the trust funds themselves are deposited with the court, the funds are secure and the trust has not been breached.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds contractors can avoid double security by paying trust funds into court, which remain secure and unappropriated under the BLA.

propositions.text: A lien bond assures payment of lien judgment but does not secure the trust claim or protect actual trust monies.
propositions.quote: A lien bond involves only an assurance that the surety will pay the amount of any lien judgment... The bond does not constitute security for the trust claim and does not result in the protection of the actual trust monies at issue.

propositions.text: Filing a lien bond requires maintaining the trust fund in addition to the bond.
propositions.quote: An owner, contractor, or subcontractor who chooses to file a lien bond with the court instead of depositing the funds at issue must maintain the trust fund in addition to the bond.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds a lien bond does not secure trust claims; trust funds must be maintained separately if a bond is filed.

propositions.text: There is no requirement to pay funds twice; payment under trust eliminates equivalent lien claim amounts.
propositions.quote: There will never be a requirement for the owner, contractor, or subcontractor to pay the funds at issue to the claimant twice.

propositions.text: Structal acknowledges paying trust monies into court could reduce the lien bond amount by equivalent monies.
propositions.quote: Structal acknowledges that, had Dominion paid the trust monies into court, there could have been a reduction in the amount of the lien bond by an amount equivalent to the monies paid into court.

propositions.text: Structal’s acknowledgment is logical; no need for lien bond to secure amount already secured by trust funds paid into court.
propositions.quote: Structal’s acknowledgment on this point is logical: there is no need for a lien bond to secure an amount already secured by trust funds paid into court.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no double payment occurs; Structal agrees trust payments reduce lien bond amounts logically.

propositions.text: Dominion chose lien bond security and paid premiums, which are unrecoverable but are the cost of chosen security.
propositions.quote: Dominion chose to provide security by way of a lien bond rather than payment of funds into court... it paid premiums for that bond which are not recoverable, but that is simply the cost of the security which it chose to provide.

propositions.text: Structal will not receive double payment.
propositions.quote: Structal will not receive double payment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Dominion paid unrecoverable premiums for lien bond security and Structal will not receive double payment.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed with costs.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal with costs. Appeal dismissed with costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal with costs.
